scams.name: Adelaide Taxi Short-Run Overcharge
scams.description:
Adelaide Airport is 7 km from the CBD's North Terrace hotels — a short, straightforward trip. At the rank, drivers say nothing unusual, run the meter, and the ride proceeds normally. The problem materializes at the destination: undisclosed charges for "fuel," "airport," and "late-night" fees that were never displayed inside the cab inflate the bill well above the expected fare.

The meter itself is sometimes the mechanism: legal rates tick in increments of $0.35 or smaller, but tampered meters click at $0.40 per increment. The difference is small per tick but compounds over a 7 km trip into a significant overcharge. Drivers who demand cash-only claim the card reader is broken; refusing the meter entirely removes the audit trail that would document the tampering.

The simplest defense is not using a taxi at all. Use Uber or DiDi from Adelaide Airport's dedicated rideshare bay — typical CBD fare $25–$40 — or take the JetExpress bus (J1, J2) from the airport to the CBD for $5.40 with a Metrocard. If you take a taxi, photograph the plate and driver ID before the trip, insist on the meter, and pay by card on the in-car terminal. Report overcharges to the South Australian Public Transport Authority at adelaidemetro.com.au.
scams.avoidance: Use Uber or DiDi from Adelaide Airport rideshare pickup — fare $25–$40 to CBD. Take JetExpress bus (J1/J2) to CBD — $5.40 with Metrocard. Pay by card on the in-car terminal and screenshot the receipt. Photograph taxi plate before the ride. Report overcharging via adelaidemetro.com.au.
scams.location: Adelaide Airport taxi rank, CBD (King William, Rundle Mall), North Terrace hotel ranks
scams.tldr: Adelaide taxi drivers — particularly from the airport rank and CBD hotel stands — run undisclosed "airport surcharges" and "fuel surcharges," and sometimes tamper meters to click at $0.40 increments instead of the legal $0.35, turning a $28 Uber-equivalent trip into a $65–$99 bill.

scams.name: DiDi / Uber 'Cancel Mid-Trip' Charge Scam
scams.description:
You book a DiDi for a short CBD trip — Rundle Mall to the Adelaide Oval, for example. The driver accepts the booking, the app confirms pickup, and you wait at the designated spot. The driver appears to arrive, briefly stops or shows as having reached your location, then the trip ends in the app with a charge showing on your card.

The receipt shows $15 for a "cancellation fee" plus "part-trip fare" — a charge for a ride you never took. The driver moved 100 metres from the pickup point, ended the trip, and headed to the next booking. A related variant has the driver call claiming an "app issue" and pressing for a direct cash payment. DiDi's customer service for disputes is notoriously slow, making the small-amount charge difficult to recover quickly.

Screenshot the app immediately when a trip ends unexpectedly. If a driver ends a trip before you reach your destination, screenshot the ride history at once and submit a refund request in-app citing the trip-end discrepancy — then escalate via your bank's chargeback process if the platform stalls. Never cancel at a driver's request; the cancellation fee flows to the driver. For CBD rides, Uber has a faster dispute process than DiDi and is worth preferring.
scams.avoidance: Never cancel at the driver's request — they're seeking a cancellation fee. Screenshot the in-app map the moment you realize the ride is being ended early. Request an in-app refund with the screenshot attached. Chargeback on your credit card if the platform denies the refund. Prefer Uber over DiDi in Adelaide for cleaner customer service.
scams.location: Adelaide CBD, DiDi and Uber platform
scams.tldr: DiDi drivers in Adelaide CBD accept a booking, drive 100 metres from the pickup point, end the trip in the app, and pocket $15 in cancellation and "part-trip" fees while leaving passengers stranded — exploiting platform fee structures designed for genuinely interrupted trips.

scams.name: Fake Barossa / McLaren Vale Wine Tour Booking
scams.description:
Searching "Barossa wine tour from Adelaide" surfaces Google Ads-funded pages that look polished and professional — four wineries, hotel pickup, lunch included, cellar-door purchases optional. The pricing of $79 is 30–40% below comparable legitimate operators. The booking process is smooth, with confirmation emails using Barossa winery imagery and plausible itinerary language naming specific wineries.

Payment is required by bank transfer "to avoid card fees" — the scam's tell. The moment the transfer clears, the operator vanishes: no minibus arrives on tour day, the phone number disconnects, and the website disappears or shows an error. Bank transfers have no built-in chargeback protection; recovery requires a formal recall request to your bank within 24 hours and a report to ScamWatch.

The payment method is the clearest warning sign. Never pay for any Adelaide tour by bank transfer or PayPal Friends & Family — always pay by credit card for chargeback protection, and book only with operators that have a physical Adelaide office and an ABN verifiable at abn.business.gov.au. Verified Barossa operators: Groovy Grape Tours (groovygrape.com.au), Taste the Barossa (tastethebarossa.com.au), Barossa Daimler (barossadaimler.com.au).
scams.avoidance: Book with Groovy Grape, Taste the Barossa, Barossa Daimler or Adelaide Wine Tours. Verify ABN at abn.business.gov.au. Pay by credit card for chargeback protection. Read 50 most recent TripAdvisor reviews — fake operators have clumped review dates. Confirm exact winery names in the itinerary before paying.
scams.location: Online via Google Ads, Facebook Ads, cloned tour booking sites
scams.tldr: Cloned wine tour sites outrank legitimate Barossa operators in Google Ads, offer full-day tours for $79 with hotel pickup and lunch, request bank transfer to "avoid card fees," and disappear on tour day — leaving visitors $79–$200 out of pocket with no recourse.

scams.name: Adelaide Fake Rental / Facebook Airbnb Invoice Scam
scams.description:
A one-bedroom listing in North Adelaide on Facebook Marketplace is priced at $120/night — below comparable Airbnb rates. The "host" is responsive, shares photos that look professional, and quickly sends what appears to be an official Airbnb invoice PDF for the full stay amount, typically $700–$1,000, complete with Airbnb branding and a booking reference number.

The invoice instructs you to bank-transfer the amount to "confirm your reservation." As soon as payment clears, the host stops responding. Airbnb has no record of the booking because the transaction was entirely outside its platform. Real Airbnb bookings are confirmed only inside the Airbnb app — the company does not send PDF invoices requesting bank transfers under any circumstances.

Airbnb's payment flow is the verification. A real Airbnb booking is confirmed entirely inside the Airbnb app — if anyone sends you an invoice PDF and requests a bank transfer, it is a scam regardless of how convincing the branding looks. Always book directly through the Airbnb app or a URL you bookmarked yourself. If you have already paid, call your bank within 24 hours and request an urgent recall.
scams.avoidance: Book only through the Airbnb or Booking.com app — never from an email link. A real Airbnb payment runs entirely in-app; external invoices are always fake. Never pay by bank transfer outside the platform. Reverse image-search listing photos in Google Images. Report scam listings to Airbnb and Facebook Marketplace immediately.
scams.location: CBD, North Adelaide, Unley, Prospect — short-stay and sharehouse market
scams.tldr: Scammers list North Adelaide short-stays on Facebook Marketplace, send a fake Airbnb-branded PDF invoice, and request bank transfer — disappearing once payment clears, with no booking record in Airbnb's platform and no refund path for bank transfers.

scams.name: International Student Visa / Education Agent Fraud
scams.description:
Prospective international students searching for Adelaide study pathways or PR sponsorship encounter social media ads and WeChat posts from "migration agents" promising streamlined visa processing and permanent residency pathways via an Adelaide-based college. Prices of $8,000–$13,000 are positioned as competitive, and the agents cite testimonials and institutional affiliations that sound plausible.

The agent takes cash upfront, providing receipts on unofficial letterhead. The college enrollment either never materializes, is issued by an institution not registered on the CRICOS register, or is later revoked — leaving the student with no valid student visa and the full amount lost. Because payment was in cash, there is no bank recall option. Adelaide's lower-cost international education market has attracted a disproportionate concentration of these schemes.

Two public registers eliminate most of the risk before you pay anything. Use only MARA-registered migration agents — searchable at mara.gov.au — and enrol only in CRICOS-registered institutions, verifiable at cricos.education.gov.au. Never pay cash for visa or education services; always pay by card or traceable bank transfer to a registered ABN with a formal receipt. Any "guaranteed PR" promise is impossible — no legitimate agent can guarantee visa outcomes.
scams.avoidance: Use only MARA-registered agents — check mara.gov.au public register. Enrol only in CRICOS-registered institutions — verify at cricos.education.gov.au. Pay by card or bank transfer with receipt — never cash. Verify agent's ABN at abn.business.gov.au. Report suspected fraud to the Department of Home Affairs at immi.gov.au.
scams.location: Online / WeChat / WhatsApp ads targeting South Asian and Southeast Asian students
scams.tldr: Unregistered "migration agents" targeting Indian and Southeast Asian students on WeChat and social media offer $8,000–$13,000 "visa pathway" packages via unaccredited Adelaide colleges — taking cash upfront and delivering an enrollment in an institution not registered on the CRICOS register.

scams.name: Fake 'SA Tourism Voucher' / Booking Voucher Scam
scams.description:
An email or Facebook ad claims you have been selected for a $100 South Australian Tourism Commission hotel voucher valid for winter stays. The site it links to closely resembles the official southaustralia.com design — SA branding, images of Barossa vineyards, and a clean booking interface. The voucher "verification" form asks for your full name, email, and card details to "confirm eligibility."

Once you submit your card information, the scammers run small test transactions — typically $1–$2 — to confirm the card is live, then proceed to larger charges. The voucher never arrives. The SA Tourism Commission did run a legitimate "Great State Voucher" program from 2020–2022, and scammers deliberately reference that period to lend credibility to the offer. The scam targets volume: small per-victim amounts across thousands of recipients.

Real government voucher programs are always announced on official .gov.au domains, never in unsolicited emails with click-through links. Verify any SA tourism voucher claim by navigating yourself directly to southaustralia.com or tourism.sa.gov.au — and never enter card details on a page you reached via an unsolicited email or SMS link. For actual Adelaide accommodation discounts, use Booking.com, Stayz, or Wotif; report phishing to ScamWatch at scamwatch.gov.au.
scams.avoidance: Verify any voucher program directly at southaustralia.com or tourism.sa.gov.au. Never click voucher links in unsolicited emails. Book hotels via Booking.com, Stayz, or calling hotels directly. If you've entered card details into a suspect site, reissue your card. Report phishing to ScamWatch at scamwatch.gov.au.
scams.location: Email / SMS / Facebook ads claiming South Australian government tourism vouchers
scams.tldr: Phishing emails and Facebook ads impersonating the "South Australian Tourism Commission" offer $100 hotel vouchers that require card details to "verify" — harvesting card numbers for small test charges followed by larger fraudulent transactions, with no voucher ever issued.
